title: Стоп-лист и признание гостьи  (The Stop-List and the Guest's Confession)

segments.t: Escalating the feud with Vika, Chef Barinov forbids the waitresses from stepping past the kitchen line and places half the menu on the stop-list. Out in the dining room, Max apologizes to his older guest, who confesses that she actually comes to Claude Monet for a certain young man.
Вы знаете, Максим, я хочу вам признаться.
Вам, видимо, нравится, как я готовлю?
Now let's break down each line of their conversation.
'Ah, so that is how you want to play it, huh?' Max probes steadily as they speak, pairing "akh" ("ah, oh") with "vot" ("there, here") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
'Now listen to my new order.' Sasha holds a resolute rhythm in front of Max, putting "teper" ("now") alongside "slushay" ("listen") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Entering is strictly forbidden.' Max sustains a warm view in their talk, putting "zakhodit" ("went in") alongside "zapreshcheno" ("to forbid, to ban") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'And just what are you going to do about it?' Sasha prompts openly in their exchange, building the phrase around "sdelayesh" ("will you make") and "chto" ("what") for a crisp, natural delivery.
'What are you doing? Quiet down!' Max asks plainly to Sasha here, leaning on "delayete" ("are doing") before closing the thought with "tikho" ("easy, quiet").
'I was not the one who started this war.' Sasha sets a sharp style during the exchange, pairing "nachala" ("beginning") with "voynu" ("the war") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
'Have you lost your minds completely?' Max quizzes calmly right away, anchoring the Russian line on "sovsem" ("at all") and "vy" ("you") without extra filler.
'Those items are on the stop-list.' Sasha adopts a pointed manner in front of Max, leaning on "stop-liste" ("86'd list") before closing the thought with "oni" ("they").
'That is quite alright, Maxim.' Sasha brings a measured direction in their talk, pairing "strashnogo" ("terrible, serious") with "nichego" ("nothing") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
Вы знаете, Максим, я хочу вам признаться.
'You know, Maxim, I want to make a confession to you.' Sasha keeps a natural mood across the room, combining "znayete" ("know") and "khochu" ("want") so the key meaning lands right away.
'Yes, I noticed that.' Max picks an honest approach as they talk, anchoring the Russian line on "zametil" ("noticed") and "da" ("yes") without extra filler.
Вам, видимо, нравится, как я готовлю?
'You apparently really like the way I cook?' Sasha tests evenly across the room, linking "vidimo" ("apparently"), "nravitsya" ("is pleasing"), and "kak" ("how") in one brisk exchange.

'I come here for the sake of one young man.' Max displays a thoughtful tempo as the scene unfolds, pairing "molodogo" ("young") with "parnya" ("boyfriend") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
Вы знаете, Максим, я хочу вам признаться.
Вам, видимо, нравится, как я готовлю?

That wraps up this scene as chef Barinov retaliates against Vika by banning waitresses from the kitchen and putting dishes on the stop-list, while the older guest hints to Max that she comes there just to see him. See you next time!
